exhibits.title: Favorite No. 20
exhibits.subtitle: J. Stevens Arms · c. 1894–1935 (Favorite family; No. 20 end date not isolated)
exhibits.summary: The smoothbore Favorite: same as the No. 17 but with a smooth barrel and no rear sight. Exists in .32 rimfire shot too, which makes it the core of our .32 honorable mention.
details: c. 1894–1935 (Favorite family; No. 20 end date not isolated)
$75–$250 (2011 Blue Book grades, 60%–100%); $150 sold (2011 Proxibid). Unverified for today's market.
sources: ATF historical Curios or Relics list, printed p. 39 (No. 20 smoothbore identification)
SASS Wire thread quoting 2001 Standard Catalog of Firearms & 2011 Blue Book (18 Jan 2012)

exhibits.title: Crack Shot No. 26½
exhibits.subtitle: J. Stevens Arms · Within No. 26 run, 1912–1939 (+1943 batch); exact 26½ years disputed
exhibits.summary: Our namesake. Stevens sold the side-lever Crack Shot from 1890 and the under-lever No. 26 from 1912; the 26½ is the same gun with a smooth bore "intended for shot cartridges." In 1902 a Crack Shot cost $2.25.
details: Within No. 26 run, 1912–1939 (+1943 batch); exact 26½ years disputed
$250 sold (iCollector, 2025). One comp only: unverified as a range. 2011 Blue Book put it about $25 under a No. 20.
sources: John Dunn, Australian Shooter, June 2020, p. 32
SASS Wire thread quoting 2001 Standard Catalog of Firearms & 2011 Blue Book (18 Jan 2012)

exhibits.title: Model 36
exhibits.subtitle: Winchester · 1920–1927
exhibits.summary: Winchester's only U.S. 9mm Flobert garden gun, roughly 20,000 made and unserialized. A cousin, not a .22, but it belongs in any shot-cartridge hall.
details: $400–$800 typical (GUNS Magazine, 2023); individual hammers to ~$1,080 reported, unverified.

exhibits.title: Model 33 Smooth Bore
exhibits.subtitle: Remington · 1932–1935 (Model 33 family; smoothbore dates not isolated)
exhibits.summary: The smoothbore story began before the 41 and 510. Remington’s historical model record names a Model 33 Smooth Bore alongside the familiar rifled single shot. Its separate shot-cartridge entry confirms a factory variant, rather than a worn-out rifled barrel.
details: Variant length not established by the factory history record
sources: Remington historical model record: Model 33 (archived July 2025)

exhibits.title: 41 SB Targetmaster
exhibits.subtitle: Remington · c. 1936–1939 (parent 41)
exhibits.summary: Remington’s history records a smoothbore in the Model 41 family and notes that the 41A smoothbore designation became 41 SB in 1938. This prewar single shot belongs alongside the Model 33 and repeating 341SB.
sources: Remington historical model record: Model 41 Targetmaster

exhibits.title: 341SB Sportmaster
exhibits.subtitle: Remington · 1936–1940 (Model 341 family; smoothbore dates not isolated)
exhibits.summary: A prewar tubular-magazine repeater in Remington’s smoothbore family. The manufacturer’s history explicitly lists the 341SB for .22 Long Rifle shot. A Remington Society account describes its bead front sight and lack of a rear sight.
details: The 2008 Standard Catalog describes a Routledge version; the factory history identifies the SB without detailing its bore profile.
sources: Remington historical model record: Model 341 (archived July 2025)

exhibits.title: Model 100SB
exhibits.subtitle: Marlin · 1936–1941
exhibits.summary: The 100SB is documented with a SMOOTH BORE – RECESS CHOKE barrel legend. Other Marlin names need care: a 1945 catalog index lists 80 CSB, while owner reports mention 80SB and 101SB. Those additional variants remain unresolved pending inspection of the original catalog pages.

exhibits.title: Model 67 Smoothbore / Miniature Target Bore
exhibits.subtitle: Winchester · SB from 1936 or 1937; Miniature Target Bore from 1940
exhibits.summary: The plain-Jane Winchester smoothbore. The Miniature Target Bore version is the rare one.

.22 S/L/LR shot; Miniature Target Bore: .22 LR shot

exhibits.title: Model 61 "Shot Only" (Routledge, later Winchester counterbore)
exhibits.subtitle: Winchester · Routledge: 1938–1939 (~75 guns); counterbore: from ~1940
exhibits.summary: The blue chip of the Hall. Early guns used Fred Routledge's stepped bore; Winchester then made its own counterbore to avoid royalties. Look for matted receivers and "FOR SHOT ONLY."
details: $3,000–$6,000 estimates (Rock Island, 2024, restored 1939 Routledge guns); $9,222.50 sold (LSB, 1951 gun, ~97%).
Routledge stepped smoothbore or later Winchester counterbore; not one uniform bore profile
sources: Westley Richards used-gun note on Routledge vs. Winchester counterbore 61s
American Rifleman: The Winchester Model 61, a historical review

exhibits.title: Model 62 Smooth Bore
exhibits.subtitle: Winchester · Documented examples around 1940; complete production dates unknown
exhibits.summary: An exception to the familiar rifled gallery pump. A collector-documented Model 62 carries a factory-style SMOOTH BORE barrel legend, and an archived specimen catalog records another as a factory smoothbore. Published collector observations establish the variant, but not a complete production total.
details: Documented examples around 1940; complete production dates unknown
The smoothbore is a separate rare variant. Ordinary Model 62 Gallery guns were rifled .22 Shorts.

exhibits.title: 121 Fieldmaster SB (Routledge bore)
exhibits.subtitle: Remington · Routledge shipments from Feb 1939; to 1954
exhibits.summary: The Mo-Skeet-O pump. Barrels stamped "ROUTLEDGE BORE," Mo-Skeet-O, or smoothbore. Routledge partnered with Remington on the bore.
details: $1,400–$1,650 sold, 2023–Jan 2026 (LSB, CT Firearms, Legacy Collectibles, Horst/HiBid).

exhibits.title: 510SB / 511SB / 512SB and 510-X SB
exhibits.subtitle: Remington · 510: 1939–1962; 511: 1939–1963; 512: 1940–1962 (parent runs); 510-X family: 1964–1966
exhibits.summary: All three SB designations appear in Remington’s historical model records: the single-shot 510, box-magazine 511 and tubular-magazine 512. The 511 record also lists a Routledge Bore variant. The dates below describe the parent models, not a proven continuous smoothbore production run. The later 510-X was also offered in Smooth Bore grade, explicitly named in Remington’s own model brochure.
details: Bolt: single shot (510), box mag (511), tube mag (512)
No dated sold comps captured (unverified); generally below 121 SB money.
510-X Smooth Bore; 1964–1966 parent family according to Remington historian John Gyde

exhibits.title: Targo: 26T, 42T, 42TR, B42T
exhibits.subtitle: O.F. Mossberg & Sons · 26T 1938–1942; 42T 1940–1942; 42TR 1940–1946 (NMCA); Targo marketed from fall 1940

.22 LR shot (42TR also bullets via RA-1 rifled muzzle adapter)

exhibits.title: Nylon 10 SB
exhibits.subtitle: Remington · 1962–1964
exhibits.summary: Remington paired a smoothbore barrel with its Mohawk-brown nylon-stocked bolt-action single shot. Blue Book gives a different total and leaves the long-barrel count unknown; no factory tally has been verified.

exhibits.summary: The single-shot member of Remington’s later bolt-action rimfire line also had a factory smoothbore variant. Remington names the 580SB in its historical record. Surviving catalogued examples show a bead sight and a barrel marked for .22 Long Rifle shot.

finale.title: Honorable mention: the .32 smoothbores
finale.plaqueSub: Stevens Favorite No. 20 & Crack Shot No. 26½ in .32 rimfire shot
body: Yes, there really was a .32. What’s confirmed: Stevens catalogued its boys’-rifle smoothbores for .32 rimfire shot cartridges as well as .22. The Favorite No. 20 was “chambered for the 22 or 32 rimfire shot cartridges and has a smoothbore barrel and no rear sight” (Standard Catalog of Firearms, 2001, as quoted), and Wikipedia lists the Crack Shot No. 26½ for “.22LR Shot Cartridges, .32 Rimfire Shot Cartridges.” The gun our club is named for came in .32 shot.
Ammo: .32 rimfire shot loads existed. A Canadian collector reports shooting a No. 20 with CIL .32 Long Shot (#10, 1935-dated). That’s one collector’s report.

Remington’s rolling blocks: A factory catalog excerpt on printed page 88 offers both the No. 4 and No. 6 with smooth bores. Separate specimen records establish .32 rimfire examples: Amoskeag’s 2019 No. 4 record describes a matching-number barrel marked SMOOTH BORE, and John Dunn photographed a No. 6 marked for .32 Short or Long rimfire with a Smooth Bore inscription beneath the barrel. These are documented examples, not proof that every family caliber was offered smooth.
Original .32 rimfire ammunition is scarce and old. Treat these guns as display pieces unless a gunsmith says otherwise.
sources: SASS Wire, 18 Jan 2012 (Standard Catalog / Blue Book quotes)
Canadian Gun Nutz: Stevens Favorite .32 Shot
Remington factory catalog excerpt, printed p. 88 (in Model 4 historical document)
Amoskeag 2019 historical catalog, lot 433: .32 RF No. 4
John Dunn, Australian Shooter, September 2020, pp. 22–24: .32 No. 6
